title: Mobility-network topology carries incremental, softness-orthogonal information about future aging dynamics in a glass-forming liquid
abstract: Does the spatial organization of particle mobility in a glass predict future motion beyond what local structure knows? In leakage-free simulations of an aging Kob--Andersen liquid ($N=2028$; 200 trajectories; three temperatures), mobility-network topology raises the out-of-fold $R^2$ by $\dRtwo=0.0049$--$0.0122$, monotonically with quench depth, retaining $\ge 98\%$ atop softness-class baselines. Giant mobile components are dense hotspots whose members subsequently quiet down: exhaustion zones of cooperative motion --- a spatial anticorrelation channel invisible to single-particle descriptors.
summary: This work investigates whether the spatial connectivity of mobile particles in a glass-forming liquid predicts future aging dynamics beyond what is known from local structure. By analyzing the 'mobility network,' the authors show that topological features carry a unique, quantifiable memory signal. This suggests that collective motion leaves a spatial imprint—an 'exhaustion zone'—that governs subsequent particle behavior.
main_problem: To determine if the spatial organization of particle mobility (mobility-network topology) in a glass-forming liquid carries predictive information about future aging dynamics beyond what is known from local, single-particle structural states.
main_result: The network topology provides a statistically significant, orthogonal predictive signal ($\Delta R^2$) for future particle motion, suggesting that collective structural memory is encoded in the spatial arrangement of mobile regions.
method: The study uses machine learning (cross-validation) on molecular dynamics simulations to quantify the predictive power of topological descriptors (like component size) derived from a mobility network, comparing this against local structural descriptors (softness).
model_or_system: The system is an aging Kob–Andersen (80:20) binary Lennard-Jones mixture simulated via LAMMPS. The analysis focuses on the dynamics of particle mobility over time windows.
key_observables: Out-of-fold $R^2$ increment ($\Delta R^2$), matched-pair difference in forward excursion ($\Delta \langle Y angle$), and hotspot-memory relaxation $\chi(s)$.
important_parameters: Quench depth (temperature), time window ($	au$), and the ratio of mobile/immobile particles defining the network.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the predictive power of the network topology is orthogonal to the information contained in the local structural fingerprint (softness).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate that the topology increment ($\Delta R^2$) is positive and increases with quench depth, and that this increment remains significant even when local structure is included, pointing to a depletion/anticorrelation mechanism in mobile regions.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by questioning if mobility organization predicts future motion. It then develops the methodology using network topology descriptors and compares the predictive power against local structure (softness). The core argument is built around demonstrating the orthogonality and physical interpretation of the network signal as an 'exhaustion zone' effect.
why_interesting: The concept of using network topology to capture non-local, collective memory in glassy dynamics is highly relevant to understanding complex energy landscapes and slow relaxation processes common in disordered quantum systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 3. The softness gate. Left: out-of-fold R2 for nested baselines (M0: state variables; M1: +14-shell fingerprint; M2: +fold-trained softness scalar; M3: +network topology). Right: the topology increment on top of the shell fingerprint (red) barely differs from its value on the weak baseline, while the fingerprint itself adds little (orange): topology is orthog- onal to local structure.

FIG. 1. Mobile-network components at T = 0.45. Top: configuration snapshot (tw = 420); gray dots are all particles, colored dots and lines are the mobile network (r < 1.5σ), with the eight largest components highlighted; the largest spans the box (71/101 mobile particles). Bottom left: component- size distributions at the three temperatures (exponential-like tails). Bottom right: mean forward excursion Y versus com- ponent size within the mobile pool (red, left axis) and mean past mobility (gray, right axis): large components are recently active hotspots whose members are subsequently quieter — exhaustion.

FIG. 2. Temperature scaling of the topology increment (N = 2028, 200 trajectories, 80 800 matched pairs per tem- perature). Left: ∆R2(τ) per temperature (solid: raw; dashed: group-centered). Middle: matched-pair difference in forward excursion, ∆⟨Y ⟩(τ). Right: best-window centered ∆R2 de- creases monotonically with T. Permutation tests give p = 0.048, 0.010, 0.048 at T = 0.45, 0.48, 0.52 (all nulls below the observed value).

FIG. 4. ∆R2 versus waiting time (fraction of the observable aging window) in both engines. (a) Quick test: N = 500, overdamped Langevin, 20 trajectories, windows τ = 2, 5 (BD units). (b) Full system: N = 2028, MD, T = 0.48, 200 trajectories, windows τ = 20, 50 (LJ units). Filled markers: permutation p < 0.10; in (b) every point sits at the permuta- tion floor. The increment is positive throughout — structural memory is maintained, not transient — and the short-over- long window ordering is reproduced at 4× the system size.
